subject: Climate & Environment
title: Illegal Logging
description: A micro-lesson that makes Illegal Logging usable.

hook.text: Up to 30% of global timber trade is estimated to come from illegal logging operations.

buildup.text: Criminal networks forge permits, bribe officials, and move logs across borders like contraband.

discovery.text: Satellite monitoring can now detect illegal clearing within days — sometimes hours.

twist.text: But enforcement is weak. Rangers in remote forests are outnumbered and sometimes killed.

climax.text: Illegal logging is worth up to $150 billion per year — rivaling the drug trade in profit.

punchline.text: Some furniture started as a crime scene in a forest.

quiz.question: What share of global timber trade comes from illegal logging?

details.summary: Illegal logging accounts for an estimated 15 to 30 percent of the global timber trade, destroying irreplaceable old-growth forests, robbing governments of billions in revenue, and often involving corruption and organized crime networks.
details.whyItMatters: Illegal logging undermines legal forestry, funds criminal networks, and strips communities and nations of natural wealth. Combating it requires both enforcement and demand-side regulation.
takeaways: Illegal logging costs producer countries 10 to 15 billion dollars per year in lost revenue
Organized crime networks drive much of the trade
Demand-side laws like the EU Timber Regulation target consuming countries

faq.question: How is illegal timber laundered into legal supply chains?
faq.answer: Illegal logs are often mixed with legal timber at sawmills, given fraudulent permits, or shipped through countries with weak oversight. Complex multi-stage supply chains make it difficult for end buyers to verify the origin of wood products.

faq.question: What technologies help detect illegal logging?
faq.answer: Satellite monitoring like Global Forest Watch detects clearing in near-real time. DNA timber tracking, isotope analysis, and blockchain-based chain-of-custody systems help verify wood origin. Drones and acoustic sensors detect chainsaw activity in protected areas.
